newsitem.title: USA: Hubble Telescope makes movie of Neptune's weather.
newsitem.headline: Hubble Telescope makes movie of Neptune's weather.

text.p: Earth's hurricanes, cyclones and typhoons are gentle compared to the wild weather on Neptune, as shown in a new movie made by the Hubble Space Telescope and another NASA telescope, scientists said on Thursday.

The film shows winds of nearly 900 mph (1,448 kmph) whipping around Neptune's equator, and the disappearance of an earlier pulsating storm known as the Great Dark Spot that was first seen on Neptune by the Voyager probe seven years ago.

The movie, made by the orbiting Hubble telescope and the Infrared Telescope Facility on a mountaintop in Hawaii, is a time-lapse account of a full 16.11 hour rotation of the planet, the scientists said.
A scientific team led by Lawrence Sromovsky at the University of Wisconsin tracked images made by the two telescopes, which are both administered by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
The cause of Neptune's violent weather, which dwarfs anything found on Earth, is a mystery, Sromovsky said in a statement.

On Earth, the third planet from the Sun, winds are driven by the Sun's energy, which heats the atmosphere and the oceans. But Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun and its energy is 900 times dimmer than on Earth, so the logical assumption would be that winds would be far weaker.
But that is the opposite of what occurs, Sromovsky said: "Neptune's weather is among the most dynamic in the solar system with changes occurring on time scales ranging from minutes to decades."
By observing Neptune's cloud movements, scientists hope to learn more about the planet's extraordinary weather, the statement said.
Sromovsky's findings were presented at the annual meeting of the Division of Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society in Tucson, Arizona.
